concepts.name: Function
concepts.statement: A function f consists of a set of inputs, a set of outputs, and a rule for assigning each input to exactly one output. When we know the input, the output is determined, so we say that the output is a function of the input.

concepts.name: Domain
concepts.statement: The domain of a function is its set of inputs. Where a function is given by an equation and no domain is stated, the domain is taken to be the set of all real numbers x for which f(x) is a real number.

concepts.name: Range
concepts.statement: The range of a function is its set of outputs: every value f(x) takes as x runs over the domain.

concepts.name: Independent variable
concepts.statement: For a function y = f(x), the input x is the independent variable.

concepts.name: Dependent variable
concepts.statement: For a function y = f(x), the output y is the dependent variable, because it depends on the input x.

concepts.name: Graph of a function
concepts.statement: The graph of a function f is the set of all points (x, y) in the coordinate plane such that x is in the domain of f and y = f(x).

concepts.name: Interval notation
concepts.statement: A set of real numbers can be described in set-builder notation, {x | x has some property}, or, when it holds every number between two endpoints, in interval notation: (a, b) leaves both endpoints out, [a, b] includes them, and ∞ and −∞, which are not real numbers, mark a side with no end.

concepts.name: Natural domain
concepts.statement: The natural domain of a function given by a formula is the set of all real numbers for which the formula gives a real output; the natural domain of f(x) = √x is the set of nonnegative real numbers.

concepts.name: Piecewise-defined function
concepts.statement: A piecewise-defined function is defined by different equations on different parts of its domain; which equation gives f(x) depends on the part of the domain in which x falls.

concepts.name: Table of values
concepts.statement: A table of values lists inputs of a function and their corresponding outputs.

concepts.name: Zeros of a function
concepts.statement: The zeros of a function f are the values of x where f(x) = 0; they are where the graph of f intersects the x-axis. A function may have any number of zeros.

concepts.name: y-intercept
concepts.statement: The y-intercept of a function f, if it exists, is the point (0, f(0)). A function has exactly one y-intercept if 0 is in its domain and none otherwise.

concepts.name: Vertical line test
concepts.statement: Given a function f, every vertical line that may be drawn intersects the graph of f no more than once. If any vertical line intersects a set of points more than once, the set of points does not represent a function.

concepts.name: Increasing on an interval
concepts.statement: A function f is increasing on the interval I if f(x₁) ≤ f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂ in I, and strictly increasing there if f(x₁) < f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂.

concepts.name: Decreasing on an interval
concepts.statement: A function f is decreasing on the interval I if f(x₁) ≥ f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂ in I, and strictly decreasing there if f(x₁) > f(x₂) whenever x₁ < x₂.

concepts.name: Combinations of functions
concepts.statement: Given two functions f and g, we can define four new functions by writing them with an operator: their sum, difference, product and quotient, the quotient only where g(x) ≠ 0. Each is defined where both f and g are.

concepts.name: Composite function
concepts.statement: If f has domain A and range B, g has domain D, and B is a subset of D, the composite function g ∘ f is the function with domain A such that (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)): f maps x to f(x), and g maps f(x) on to g(f(x)). The order in which we compose functions matters.

concepts.name: Symmetry about the y-axis
concepts.statement: The graph of a function f is symmetric about the y-axis if (−x, y) is on the graph whenever (x, y) is: the part of the curve to the right of the y-axis, flipped over it, lies exactly on the part to the left.

concepts.name: Symmetry about the origin
concepts.statement: The graph of a function f is symmetric about the origin if (−x, −y) is on the graph whenever (x, y) is: rotated 180° about the origin, the graph looks exactly the same.

concepts.name: Even function
concepts.statement: A function f is even if f(−x) = f(x) for all x in its domain. An even function is symmetric about the y-axis.

concepts.name: Odd function
concepts.statement: A function f is odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for all x in its domain. An odd function is symmetric about the origin.

concepts.name: Absolute value function
concepts.statement: The absolute value function |x| is −x for x < 0 and x for x ≥ 0. Its output is positive for every nonzero input and 0 at x = 0, so its range is {y | y ≥ 0}; it is symmetric about the y-axis and so even.

concepts.name: Slope
concepts.statement: The slope of a line through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = Δy/Δx, the change in y for each unit change in x. For a line it does not depend on which two points are chosen.

concepts.name: Linear function
concepts.statement: A linear function is one that can be written in the form f(x) = mx + b; its graph is a line with slope m.

concepts.name: Point-slope equation
concepts.statement: The point-slope equation of the line through (x₁, y₁) with slope m is y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

concepts.name: Slope-intercept form
concepts.statement: The equation of the line with slope m and y-intercept (0, b) in slope-intercept form is y = mx + b.

concepts.name: Standard form of a line
concepts.statement: The standard form of a line is ax + by = c, where a and b are not both zero; it is more general than the other forms because it allows a vertical line, x = k.

concepts.name: Polynomial function
concepts.statement: A polynomial function is any function that can be written as f(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁x + a₀ for some integer n ≥ 0 and constants aₙ, …, a₀ with aₙ ≠ 0; if every coefficient is 0 it is the zero function.

concepts.name: Degree
concepts.statement: The degree of a polynomial function is the value n of the largest exponent of any of its terms.

concepts.name: Leading coefficient
concepts.statement: The leading coefficient of a polynomial of degree n is the constant aₙ that multiplies xⁿ.

concepts.name: Constant function
concepts.statement: A polynomial of degree 0, f(x) = a₀, is a constant function; its graph is a horizontal line.

concepts.name: Quadratic function
concepts.statement: A quadratic function is a polynomial of degree 2, f(x) = ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0; its graph is a parabola, opening upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0.

concepts.name: Cubic function
concepts.statement: A cubic function is a polynomial of degree 3, f(x) = ax³ + bx² + cx + d with a ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Power function
concepts.statement: A power function is any function of the form f(x) = axᵇ, where a and b are real numbers. When the exponent is a positive integer n, axⁿ is a polynomial, even if n is even and odd if n is odd.

concepts.name: End behavior of a polynomial
concepts.statement: The end behavior of a function is what happens to f(x) as x → ∞ and as x → −∞. A polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 satisfies f(x) → ±∞ as x → ±∞, and its leading term decides which: the sign of the leading coefficient and whether n is even or odd.

concepts.name: Quadratic formula
concepts.statement: The solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 are x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). If the discriminant b² − 4ac is positive there are two real solutions, if it is zero there is one, and if it is negative there is none.

concepts.name: Mathematical model
concepts.statement: A mathematical model is a method of simulating a real-life situation with mathematical equations, such as a function fitted to collected data.

concepts.name: Algebraic function
concepts.statement: An algebraic function is one that involves only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, rational powers and roots applied to the input variable x.

concepts.name: Rational function
concepts.statement: A rational function is a quotient of polynomials, f(x) = p(x)/q(x); its domain is the set of x with q(x) ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Root function
concepts.statement: A root function is a power function f(x) = x^{1/n} for an integer n ≥ 2. Its domain is [0, ∞) if n is even and (−∞, ∞) if n is odd, and for odd n it is an odd function.

concepts.name: Transcendental function
concepts.statement: A transcendental function is one that cannot be described by basic algebraic operations; the most common are the trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions.

concepts.name: Exponential function
concepts.statement: An exponential function is a function of the form f(x) = bˣ, where the base b > 0 and b ≠ 1. It is increasing if b > 1 and decreasing if 0 < b < 1, with domain (−∞, ∞) and range (0, ∞).

concepts.name: Logarithmic function
concepts.statement: A logarithmic function is a function f(x) = log_b(x) for some base b > 0, b ≠ 1, where log_b(x) = y if and only if bʸ = x. It is the inverse of y = bˣ, with domain (0, ∞) and range (−∞, ∞).

concepts.name: Transformation of a function
concepts.statement: A transformation of a function is a shift, scaling or reflection of its graph: f(x) + c shifts it up c units, f(x + c) left c units, cf(x) scales it vertically and f(cx) horizontally by a factor of c, and −f(x) and f(−x) reflect it about the x- and y-axes. The graph of y = cf(a(x + b)) + d comes from that of y = f(x) by the horizontal shift, the horizontal scaling, the vertical scaling and the vertical shift, in that order.

concepts.name: Radian
concepts.statement: The radian measure of an angle θ is the length s of the arc it cuts off on the unit circle, so the angle of an arc of length 1 has radian measure 1. An angle of 180° has a radian measure of π rad.

concepts.name: Trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: For a point P = (x, y) on the unit circle and the angle θ from the positive x-axis to OP, sin θ = y, cos θ = x, tan θ = y/x, csc θ = 1/y, sec θ = 1/x and cot θ = x/y, wherever the quotient is defined. On a circle of radius r they are the same ratios with x/r and y/r, and for an acute angle they are ratios of two sides of a right triangle.

concepts.name: Trigonometric identity
concepts.statement: A trigonometric identity is an equation involving trigonometric functions that is true for all angles θ for which the functions in it are defined.

concepts.name: Reciprocal and ratio identities
concepts.statement: The cotangent, cosecant and secant are the reciprocals of the tangent, sine and cosine, and the tangent and cotangent are the ratios of sine and cosine.

concepts.name: Pythagorean identities
concepts.statement: For every angle θ where the functions are defined, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

concepts.name: Addition and subtraction formulas
concepts.statement: The sine and cosine of a sum or difference of two angles are given by the sines and cosines of the angles.

concepts.name: Double-angle formulas
concepts.statement: The sine and cosine of twice an angle: sin(2θ) = 2 sin θ cos θ and cos(2θ) = 2cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2sin²θ = cos²θ − sin²θ.

concepts.name: Periodic function
concepts.statement: A function is periodic if it has a repeating pattern as the values of x move from left to right. The trigonometric functions are periodic, since θ and θ + 2π correspond to the same point of the unit circle.

concepts.name: Period
concepts.statement: The period of a function f is the smallest positive value p such that f(x + p) = f(x) for all x in its domain. Sine, cosine, secant and cosecant have period 2π; tangent and cotangent have period π.

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.statement: For a transformed sine or cosine f(x) = A sin(B(x − α)) + C, the factor A stretches the graph vertically by |A|, and |A| is called the amplitude of f.

concepts.name: Generalized sine function
concepts.statement: A transformed sine function f(x) = A sin(B(x − α)) + C has amplitude |A| and period 2π/|B|; α shifts its graph horizontally, a phase shift, and C shifts it vertically. A cosine is a sine shifted left π/2 units.

concepts.name: One-to-one function
concepts.statement: A function f is one-to-one if f(x₁) ≠ f(x₂) when x₁ ≠ x₂: no two inputs are sent to the same output.

concepts.name: Inverse function
concepts.statement: Given a function f with domain D and range R, its inverse function, if it exists, is the function f⁻¹ with domain R and range D such that f⁻¹(y) = x if f(x) = y. A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one.

concepts.name: Horizontal line test
concepts.statement: A function f is one-to-one if and only if every horizontal line intersects the graph of f no more than once.

concepts.name: Finding an inverse function
concepts.statement: To find the inverse of a one-to-one function, solve the equation y = f(x) for x, then interchange the variables x and y and write y = f⁻¹(x).

concepts.name: Graph of an inverse function
concepts.statement: If (a, b) is on the graph of f, then (b, a) is on the graph of f⁻¹, so the graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f about the line y = x.

concepts.name: Restricted domain
concepts.statement: A restricted domain is a subset of the domain of a function. A function that is not one-to-one can be restricted to a smaller domain on which it is, and its inverse defined there.

concepts.name: Inverse trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: The inverse trigonometric functions are the inverses of the trigonometric functions on restricted domains where they are one-to-one: sin⁻¹ x = y if sin y = x and −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, cos⁻¹ x = y if cos y = x and 0 ≤ y ≤ π, both for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1, and similarly for tan⁻¹, cot⁻¹, csc⁻¹ and sec⁻¹.

concepts.name: Base
concepts.statement: The base is the number b in the exponential function f(x) = bˣ and the logarithmic function f(x) = log_b x.

concepts.name: Exponent
concepts.statement: The exponent is the value x in the expression bˣ.

concepts.name: Laws of exponents
concepts.statement: For any constants a > 0, b > 0 and all x and y: bˣ·bʸ = bˣ⁺ʸ, bˣ/bʸ = bˣ⁻ʸ, (bˣ)ʸ = bˣʸ, (ab)ˣ = aˣbˣ and aˣ/bˣ = (a/b)ˣ.

concepts.name: Compound interest
concepts.statement: P dollars invested at an annual interest rate r, compounded n times per year, grow to A(t) = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ after t years; compounded continuously, to A(t) = Pe^{rt}.

concepts.name: The number e
concepts.statement: As m gets larger, the quantity (1 + 1/m)ᵐ gets closer to some real number, and we define that number to be e; to six decimal places, e ≈ 2.718282.

concepts.name: Natural exponential function
concepts.statement: The natural exponential function is f(x) = eˣ, the exponential function with base e. It is the only exponential function whose tangent line at x = 0 has slope 1.

concepts.name: Natural logarithm
concepts.statement: The natural logarithm is the logarithm with base e, ln x = log_e x, the inverse of the natural exponential function: ln(eˣ) = x for all x and e^{ln x} = x for x > 0.

concepts.name: Common logarithm
concepts.statement: The common logarithm is the logarithm with base 10, written log₁₀ or log.

concepts.name: Properties of logarithms
concepts.statement: If a, b, c > 0, b ≠ 1, and r is any real number, then log_b(ac) = log_b(a) + log_b(c), log_b(a/c) = log_b(a) − log_b(c) and log_b(aʳ) = r log_b(a): the product, quotient and power properties.

concepts.name: Change-of-base formulas
concepts.statement: For a > 0, b > 0, a ≠ 1 and b ≠ 1, aˣ = b^{x log_b a} for any real x and log_a x = log_b x / log_b a for x > 0, so an exponential or logarithmic function in any base can be written in base e.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: The hyperbolic functions sinh, cosh, tanh, csch, sech and coth involve combinations of eˣ and e⁻ˣ: cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2 and sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, and the other four are their quotients and reciprocals.

concepts.name: Identities involving hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: The hyperbolic functions satisfy identities like the trigonometric ones: cosh is even and sinh odd, cosh x ± sinh x = e^{±x}, cosh²x − sinh²x = 1, and sums of arguments expand as for sine and cosine.

concepts.name: Inverse hyperbolic functions
concepts.statement: The inverse hyperbolic functions are the inverses of the hyperbolic functions, cosh and sech restricted to [0, ∞); each can be written as a composition of the natural logarithm and an algebraic function.

concepts.name: Rate of change
concepts.statement: The rate of change of a function measures how fast its values change as its input changes; for a linear function it is constant and given by the slope, but no single number gives it for a nonlinear function.

concepts.name: Secant
concepts.statement: The secant to the function f(x) through the points (a, f(a)) and (x, f(x)) is the line passing through these points; its slope estimates the rate of change of f at a, and the estimate improves as x gets closer to a.

concepts.name: Tangent
concepts.statement: A tangent line to the graph of a function at a point (a, f(a)) is the line that secant lines through (a, f(a)) approach as they are taken through points on the function with x-values that approach a; its slope measures the rate of change of the function at a, the derivative f′(a).

concepts.name: Tangent problem
concepts.statement: The tangent problem asks how to determine the slope of a line tangent to a curve at a point; it is solved by letting x approach a in the slope of the secant line, and it led to differential calculus.

concepts.name: Differential calculus
concepts.statement: Differential calculus is the field of calculus concerned with the study of derivatives and their applications.

concepts.name: Average velocity
concepts.statement: The average velocity of an object over a time period is the change in its position divided by the length of the time period: for a position s(t), over [a, t] it is (s(t) − s(a))/(t − a), the slope of a secant line to s.

concepts.name: Limit
concepts.statement: Letting x or t approach a in an expression is called taking a limit; the limit of a function f(x) as x approaches a is the value that f(x) approaches as x approaches a.

concepts.name: Instantaneous velocity
concepts.statement: For a position function s(t), the instantaneous velocity at a time t = a is the value that the average velocities approach on intervals of the form [a, t] and [t, a] as the values of t become closer to a, provided such a value exists.

concepts.name: Area problem
concepts.statement: The area problem asks how to find the area between the graph of a function and the x-axis over an interval [a, b]; the area is approximated by the sum of the areas of thin rectangles, and as their widths approach zero the sums approach the area, a limit that underlies the definite integral.

concepts.name: Integral calculus
concepts.statement: Integral calculus is the study of integrals and their applications.

concepts.name: Multivariable calculus
concepts.statement: Multivariable calculus is the study of the calculus of functions of two or more variables, such as motion in space and the volumes of solids under surfaces.

concepts.name: Intuitive definition of the limit
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be defined at all values in an open interval containing a, with the possible exception of a itself, and let L be a real number. If all values of f(x) approach L as the values of x (≠ a) approach a, then the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L: as x gets closer to a, f(x) gets closer and stays close to L.

concepts.name: Evaluating a limit with a table
concepts.statement: To estimate the limit of f(x) as x approaches a, make a table of functional values for x approaching a from below and from above (a ± 0.1, a ± 0.01, …); if both columns approach a common value L, the limit is L, which a graph traced near a can confirm.

concepts.name: Two important limits
concepts.statement: For a real number a and a constant c, the limit of x as x approaches a is a, and the limit of the constant c is c.

concepts.name: Existence of a limit
concepts.statement: For the limit of a function to exist at a point, the functional values must approach a single real number there; if they do not, the limit does not exist (DNE), as for sin(1/x) as x approaches 0.

concepts.name: One-sided limit
concepts.statement: A one-sided limit is a limit taken from either the left or the right: L is the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left if the values f(x) approach L as x < a approaches a, and from the right if they approach L as x > a approaches a.

concepts.name: Relating one-sided and two-sided limits
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be defined at all values in an open interval containing a, with the possible exception of a, and let L be a real number. Then the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L if and only if the limits from the left and from the right are both L.

forms.latex: \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\;\text{if and only if}\;\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L\;\text{and}\;\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L

concepts.name: Infinite limit
concepts.statement: A function has an infinite limit at a point a if its values increase or decrease without bound as x approaches a, from the left, from the right or from both sides; writing that the limit is +∞ or −∞ describes this behavior and does not assert that a limit exists.

concepts.name: Infinite limits from positive integers
concepts.statement: For a positive integer n, 1/(x − a)ⁿ has an infinite limit at a: +∞ from both sides if n is even; +∞ from the right and −∞ from the left if n is odd.

concepts.name: Vertical asymptote
concepts.statement: The line x = a is a vertical asymptote of f(x) if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left, from the right or from both sides is +∞ or −∞.

concepts.name: Sum law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a sum is the sum of the limits: L + M.

concepts.name: Difference law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a difference is the difference of the limits: L − M.

concepts.name: Constant multiple law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a constant c times a function is c times its limit: cL.

concepts.name: Product law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a product is the product of the limits: L · M.

concepts.name: Quotient law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, L/M, provided M ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Power law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of the nth power of a function is the nth power of its limit, Lⁿ, for every positive integer n.

concepts.name: Root law for limits
concepts.statement: Where the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are L and M. The limit of the nth root of a function is the nth root of its limit, for all L if n is odd and for L ≥ 0 if n is even and f(x) ≥ 0.

concepts.name: Limit laws
concepts.statement: The limit laws are the individual properties of limits: for f(x) and g(x) defined for all x ≠ a over some open interval containing a, with limits L and M at a, and a constant c, the limit of a sum, difference, constant multiple, product, quotient (M ≠ 0), power or root is that combination of L and M.

concepts.name: Limits of polynomial and rational functions
concepts.statement: For polynomials p(x) and q(x) and a real number a, the limit of p(x) as x approaches a is p(a), and the limit of p(x)/q(x) is p(a)/q(a) when q(a) ≠ 0: such limits are found by direct substitution.

concepts.name: Limits of functions equal near a
concepts.statement: If f(x) = g(x) for all x ≠ a over some open interval containing a, then the limits of f(x) and g(x) as x approaches a are equal.

concepts.name: Indeterminate form 0/0
concepts.statement: A limit of f(x)/g(x) as x approaches a where the limits of f(x) and g(x) are both 0 has the indeterminate form 0/0: substitution gives no value, and the limit may still exist.

concepts.name: Evaluating a 0/0 limit
concepts.statement: To evaluate a limit of f(x)/g(x) with the indeterminate form 0/0, find a function equal to it for all x ≠ a near a, by factoring and canceling, multiplying by a conjugate where a square root is involved, or simplifying a complex fraction, then apply the limit laws.

concepts.name: Squeeze theorem
concepts.statement: Let f(x), g(x) and h(x) be defined for all x ≠ a over an open interval containing a. If f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) for all x ≠ a in that interval and the limits of f(x) and h(x) as x approaches a are both the real number L, then the limit of g(x) is L.

concepts.name: Important trigonometric limits
concepts.statement: As θ approaches 0, sin θ approaches 0, cos θ approaches 1, sin θ/θ approaches 1 and (1 − cos θ)/θ approaches 0; the squeeze theorem on the unit circle, where sin θ < θ < tan θ for 0 < θ < π/2, establishes them.

concepts.name: Continuity at a point
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is continuous at a point a if and only if f(a) is defined, the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists, and that limit equals f(a); intuitively, its graph has no break at a.

concepts.name: Discontinuity at a point
concepts.statement: A function is discontinuous at a point, or has a discontinuity at the point, if it is not continuous there.

concepts.name: Determining continuity at a point
concepts.statement: To decide whether f is continuous at a: check that f(a) is defined; compute the limit of f(x) as x approaches a, through the one-sided limits if needed, and check that it exists; compare it with f(a). A failure at any step means f is not continuous at a.

concepts.name: Continuity of polynomials and rational functions
concepts.statement: Polynomials and rational functions are continuous at every point in their domains.

concepts.name: Removable discontinuity
concepts.statement: A function f discontinuous at a has a removable discontinuity at a if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists; its graph has a hole there.

concepts.name: Jump discontinuity
concepts.statement: A function f discontinuous at a has a jump discontinuity at a if the limits of f(x) from the left and from the right both exist as real numbers but are not equal.

concepts.name: Infinite discontinuity
concepts.statement: A function f discontinuous at a has an infinite discontinuity at a if its limit from the left or from the right is +∞ or −∞; it lies at a vertical asymptote.

concepts.name: Continuity from the right
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is continuous from the right at a if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the right is f(a).

concepts.name: Continuity from the left
concepts.statement: A function f(x) is continuous from the left at a if the limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the left is f(a).

concepts.name: Continuity over an interval
concepts.statement: A function is continuous over an open interval if it is continuous at every point in it, and over a closed interval [a, b] if it is continuous at every point of (a, b), continuous from the right at a and from the left at b; its graph can then be traced without lifting the pencil.

concepts.name: Composite function theorem
concepts.statement: If f(x) is continuous at L and the limit of g(x) as x approaches a is L, then the limit of f(g(x)) as x approaches a is f(L).

concepts.name: Continuity of trigonometric functions
concepts.statement: Trigonometric functions are continuous over their entire domains.

concepts.name: Intermediate Value Theorem
concepts.statement: Let f be continuous over a closed, bounded interval [a, b]. If z is any real number between f(a) and f(b), then there is a number c in [a, b] satisfying f(c) = z.

concepts.name: Epsilon-delta definition of the limit
concepts.statement: Let f(x) be defined for all x ≠ a over an open interval containing a, and let L be a real number. Then the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L if, for every ε > 0, there exists a δ > 0 such that if 0 < |x − a| < δ, then |f(x) − L| < ε.

concepts.name: Proving a limit with epsilon and delta
concepts.statement: To prove that the limit of a specific f(x) as x approaches a is L: let ε > 0; choose δ, found algebraically or geometrically from |f(x) − L| < ε; assume 0 < |x − a| < δ; use it to show |f(x) − L| < ε; conclude that the limit is L.

concepts.name: Triangle inequality
concepts.statement: The triangle inequality states that if a and b are any real numbers, then |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.

concepts.name: A limit that does not exist
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a does not exist if for every real number L there exists ε > 0 so that for all δ > 0 there is an x satisfying 0 < |x − a| < δ with |f(x) − L| ≥ ε.

concepts.name: Epsilon-delta one-sided limits
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a from the right is L if for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that 0 < x − a < δ implies |f(x) − L| < ε; from the left, −δ < x − a < 0 replaces 0 < x − a < δ.

concepts.name: Epsilon-delta infinite limits
concepts.statement: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a is +∞ if for every M > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ implies f(x) > M, and −∞ if it implies f(x) < −M.
